extracted.intended_audience: New York Times journalists, editors, and newsroom staff
extracted.subtask_description: The Times' newsroom standards for producing and publishing news: guidance on verification, handling rumors and anonymous sources, conflicts of interest, corrections, fairness, and implicit tests of newsworthiness and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "Enhance society by creating, collecting and distributing high-quality news and information." Producing content of the highest quality and integrity is the basis for reputation and fulfilling public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this mission as the primary touchstone for editorial choices: prioritize public service, quality, and integrity in deciding what to publish and how to report it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are their own principal fact-checkers. Concrete facts (addresses, titles, distances, phone numbers) must be verified. Standard references required (directories, official sites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should verify basic, checkable facts themselves rather than relying solely on others; use authoritative reference sources for routine factual details to avoid errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rumors and Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rumors must satisfy The Times's standard of newsworthiness, taste and plausibility before publication, even when attributed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply The Times's three-pronged test—newsworthiness, taste, plausibility—before publishing rumored material; attribution alone does not make a rumor publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Times's three-pronged test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times's three-pronged test: newsworthiness, taste, plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential items against all three dimensions: (1) Is it of public interest? (2) Is publishing it tasteful — avoiding gratuitous sensationalism? (3) Is the claim plausible given available evidence?

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid real or apparent conflicts with sources, advertisers, advocacy groups; consider family/spouse civic activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose and manage any relationships or activities that might bias reporting or create the appearance of bias; recuse or obtain editorial oversight when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, prompt correction of all errors; prominent, consistent location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish clear corrections quickly when mistakes occur and place them where readers will consistently find them to maintain transparency and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttals & Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticism is serious, NYT has a "special obligation" to describe scope and allow subject to respond; multi-source confirmation for damaging claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give subjects of serious criticism a chance to respond and seek corroboration from multiple sources before publishing claims that could damage reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous sources are a last resort, not first; editor approval required; reasoning explained to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anonymity only when essential to obtain information in the public interest, secure explicit editorial sign-off, and explain to readers why anonymity was granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality / craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Highest editorial standards of writing, reporting, and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize excellent journalism craft—clear writing, solid reporting, rigorous editing—as integral to newsworthiness and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity / verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts must check out; reporting should be verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize verifiable information and transparent sourcing so readers can assess the basis for reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness as a standalone test for whether material should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public significance and relevance when deciding to publish; not all true or interesting things are newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraint on sensational, sexual, or violent content; consider societal standards of decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous details or sensationalism that serve no public-interest purpose; weigh harm and dignity of subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude implausible claims; require believable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skeptically vet claims that strain credulity and demand stronger verification before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration and fair treatment of people who are the subject of negative coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reporting describes scope, gives opportunity to respond, and avoids unfairly prejudicial framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a diversity of sources rather than a single perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek multiple, independent voices to provide balance and corroboration, especially on contentious issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether reporting serves the public interest or has public impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories that inform citizens, expose wrongdoing, or otherwise contribute to public understanding and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service to public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should serve and sustain the public's trust in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make decisions that reinforce credibility, transparency, and accountability to readers.
